author: Mo Qureshi
headline: Food and pharmaceuticals lead Saudi Industry Forum programme axes
deck: The first of nine programme axes reflects an industrial base quite different from the Eastern Province's.
excerpt: Food and pharmaceutical industries lead the Saudi Industry Forum's nine programme axes, reflecting the western region's distinct industrial composition.
content:
The Saudi Industry Forum opens at the Jeddah Superdome on 14 September with nine declared programme axes, and the first of them is food and pharmaceutical industries. The ordering is not accidental, and it reflects a regional industrial composition that differs materially from the one usually described when Saudi manufacturing is discussed.

The Kingdom's industrial identity is dominated in most accounts by the Eastern Province: hydrocarbons, petrochemicals, refining, metals and the heavy fabrication that serves them. That complex is real and it is where the largest single investments sit. It is not, however, what the western region principally makes.

Jeddah and its hinterland have historically been oriented toward consumer goods, food processing, pharmaceuticals, packaging and the port-facing trade that supports them. The reasons are geographic. Jeddah Islamic Port is the Kingdom's principal Red Sea gateway and handles a large share of imported food and raw materials; the western region carries a substantial population concentration; and Makkah and Madinah generate demand of a scale and seasonality that supports dedicated supply chains in food service and consumer products.

That composition explains several of the forum's other axes too. Perfumes and cosmetics is an unusual thing to find on a national industrial agenda and makes sense as a western-region sector with established local manufacturing. Logistics follows from the port. Advanced transformation industries and innovative manufacturing technologies are the general categories, and automotive and renewable energy reflect national programmes rather than regional strengths.

The pharmaceutical axis carries the most policy weight of the group. Domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing is a security consideration in the same way food processing is — a country that formulates and packages medicines domestically is less exposed than one importing finished product — and it requires regulatory capability, sterile manufacturing facilities and quality systems that take years to establish. It is also a sector where localisation is genuinely difficult for the reasons this publication has observed elsewhere: the deliverable is a regulated capability rather than a physical component.

Saudi Food Manufacturing follows at the same venue on 27 September, which gives the Jeddah Superdome two industrial events in a month addressing overlapping constituencies. Whether that is complementary or competing for the same exhibitors is a fair question.

The forum is held under the patronage of Prince Khalid Al-Faisal bin Abdulaziz, Governor of Makkah Region, and organised by the Federation of Saudi Chambers with the Jeddah Chamber, in strategic partnership with the Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources. Its 2025 edition delivered 320-plus exhibitors and 78 speakers.

Programme axes are taken from the organiser's published material; no speaker names or session titles had been released.
